money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: Croatia's currency is the euro (EUR). If you're travelling to or from any non-EU country, declare cash of more than 10,000 euros or equivalent. This covers all forms of currency, not only cash. If you fail to declare it or give wrong information, you'll be fined and the funds may be confiscated. You don't need to declare currency if you're travelling to or from another EU country.

laws.rule: Possessing, using or trafficking illicit drugs is illegal. If you're arrested for a drug offence, police may detain you while they investigate. Penalties include imprisonment.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Police issue on-the-spot fines for some minor offences, including traffic violations. They may detain you and/or hold your passport if you: challenge the offence can't pay the fine
laws.heading: On-the-spot fines

laws.rule: Foreigners buying property have been involved in lengthy disputes about the validity of property titles. Seek independent legal advice before signing any contracts.
laws.heading: Property laws

laws.rule: You must carry an ID, such as your passport, at all times. You must register your stay with the local police within 48 hours of arrival. If you're staying at a hotel or a tourist facility, the accommodation provider will register you. Drinking alcohol in public areas, outside bars and restaurants, and in popular tourist areas such as Split and Dubrovnik is prohibited. Signs warning of prohibited behaviours, including drunken and disorderly behaviour, have been put up, and on-the-spot fines are issued. Dress codes apply. Police may fine you if you're shirtless or wearing swimwear in towns with signs banning this.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Court staff take holidays over the summer. If you're detained at that time, you may face delays in having your case processed. You may not be able to leave Croatia until the matter is finalised.
laws.heading: Court holidays

laws.rule: To drive a vehicle, you'll need both: a current Australian driver's licence, and a valid international driving permit (IDP) Driving without an IDP could void your travel and vehicle insurance. If you plan to live in Croatia, you must exchange your Australian driver's licence for a Croatian one within 12 months of arrival. You can do this at the local police station.
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: Anyone entering or leaving the European Union with cash worth EUR 10,000 or more (about A$15,900 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026, A$1 = EUR 0.6293) must declare it to customs. Cash here means banknotes and coins, bearer cheques and similar instruments, gold and other commodities used as stores of value, and prepaid cards. Each member state sets its own penalty for not declaring; the EU regulation says penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
laws.heading: Cash declaration (EU Regulation 2018/1672)

laws.rule: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU duty-free allowance is 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus one of: 1 litre of spirits over 22% alcohol, or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine. The EU page tells travellers to check the destination country's customs for the latest limits.
laws.heading: Duty-free alcohol from outside the EU

laws.rule: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU allowance is 200 cigarettes, 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco. The EU page says a lower limit (40 cigarettes, 20 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50 g of tobacco) applies to land and sea travellers in some EU countries; check this country's customs. You can mix product types but the total must stay within the limit.
laws.heading: Duty-free tobacco from outside the EU

laws.rule: Travelling into the EU from a non-EU country, you are not allowed to bring any meat or dairy products. Limited amounts of fruit and vegetables, eggs, egg products, honey and some fish are allowed. Exceptions: up to 10 kg per person from the Faroe Islands or Greenland, and up to 2 kg of powdered infant milk, infant food or special medical foods (unopened, shelf-stable, proprietary brand), or health-related pet food for an accompanying pet. Undeclared products are confiscated and destroyed, and a fine or prosecution is possible.
laws.heading: Meat and dairy from outside the EU

laws.rule: Under Article 75 of the Schengen Convention, a traveller carrying narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances for their own medical treatment must be able to produce, at a check, a certificate issued or authenticated by a competent authority of their state of residence. The certificate form covers the substance, quantity and length of the journey. How a resident of Australia obtains one is not checked in this entry; ask this country's embassy or health authority before travel.
laws.heading: Schengen certificate for narcotic or psychotropic medicines (Article 75)

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Split's Public Order Act (published by the Split tourist board): EUR 300 fines for drinking alcohol in public in the historic centre or within 100 m of schools, climbing or sitting on monuments, bathing in fountains, vomiting or relieving yourself in public; EUR 150 for sleeping in parks and public spaces. Other coastal towns set their own rules. Carry your passport. Some town centres, including Split and Dubrovnik, give on-the-spot fines for drinking in public, sleeping in public, walking around shirtless or in swimwear, and climbing on monuments; public order offences such as shouting, drunkenness or insulting officials can bring fines up to 4,000 euros. Beware of unexploded mines in former war areas away from tourist resorts.

visa-preparation.before_departure: Nothing to lodge before travel today: EES registration happens at the border. ETIAS hadn't started on 2026-11-01.
steps: Croatia is in the Schengen area: short stays of 90 days or less can be visa-free in some cases; other purposes or longer stays need a visa before travel.
At the first Schengen border, give fingerprints and a photo for the Entry/Exit System (EES). It's free; nothing is needed before arrival, and sites charging for it are fraudulent.
Carry your passport when crossing borders, including inside Schengen (temporary internal checks are in place in places).
Get a clear entry stamp at the first Schengen entry.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: EU baseline (EASA): register once as an operator in the state of residence or establishment, recognised across EASA states; Specific-category work in another state needs cross-border acceptance by that state's authority. National register, zone map and visitor rules checked 6 Nov 2026 (see items); footage routes not yet checked.

items.text: Not yet checked: whether the national aviation authority publishes a list of authorised operators.

EU rules (Regulations 2019/947 and 2019/945): operators register in the EASA state where they reside or are established; Specific-category operations need an operational authorisation or a standard-scenario declaration.

An operator registered in another EASA state may fly here; for Specific-category work it first gets the authorisation or STS declaration at home, then the destination authority must confirm the cross-border operation before flying. Rules for operators from outside EASA states: not yet checked.
Not yet checked: national tourism board or film commission media libraries.

The CCAA (Croatian Civil Aviation Agency) registers operators on its drone portal (drone.ccaa.hr). Registration is not needed for a drone under 250 g at take-off with no sensor such as a camera or microphone. Registration also requires aviation liability insurance.
The CCAA says EU residents register at home and that is recognised in Croatia; non-EU visitors register in the first EU state where they plan to fly, which is Croatia if they start there.

HTZ's image galleries, per a search summary, let journalists publish photographs to promote Croatia with the photographer and Croatian Tourist Board credited; other uses need HTZ's approval. Video, aerial footage and registration were not confirmed.
